articles.title: A New – and Old – China Human Rights Agenda at the United Nations
articles.full_text:
Why did China support the re-election of Volker Turk as U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights?
Volker Türk, United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, addresses the informal meeting of the General Assembly plenary to hear a briefing on missing persons, Apr. 2, 2025.
Volker Turk, the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, has won re-election to hold that post for another four years. Several governments objected to the process; 144 others, including China, voted in support of a second term for him.
Over the past four years Chinese authorities have deepened repression. The Chinese government inflicts collective punishment on the families of defenders and prisoners of conscience and has a disturbing track record of defenders dying in detention. Its enthusiasm for transnational repression – an effort to silence critics of the Chinese government outside the country – is growing, and it increasingly thwarts human rights scrutiny by U.N. bodies. In fact, the Chinese government ranks high among the states targeting human rights defenders for engaging with U.N. human rights mechanisms. 
While Turk has offered up occasional critiques of Beijing’s human rights abuses, ranging from calling for abusive laws to be repealed and condemning the treatment of individual prisoners of conscience, his efforts have caused Beijing no real discomfort, and not kept pace with that regime’s violations.
Just weeks before Turk formally took up the role of High Commissioner in October 2022, the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) published a landmark report alleging that Chinese government policies toward Uyghurs and other Turkic communities entailed mass arbitrary detention, torture, and family separations. The report concluded that the Chinese government’s actions “may… constitute crimes against humanity.” 
Pressed by governments, journalists, and activists since then, Turk has said that there “is no crack of light” between him and the report’s findings. Yet over the past four years, he and his senior colleagues opted to pursue the diplomatic cul-de-sac of dialogues with those responsible for the abuses: Chinese government officials. He has rarely met with the victims and survivors of Beijing’s abuses.
Turk cannot now say that he needs time to cycle through the standard diplomatic playbook with Beijing – those efforts do not appear to have yielded results, allowing further human rights deteriorations to go unaddressed. If in his second term he wants to make meaningful progress toward redressing deepening repression inside China – and halting Chinese government abuses in other countries – he should prioritize four steps, all of them immediately achievable.
First, when the U.N. Human Rights Council – the world’s flagship political human rights body – goes into session in September, Turk should seize the opportunity to brief member states on what he has tried to achieve for victims and survivors since that September 2022 report. He should explain why those efforts have faltered, and, most importantly, what he plans to do instead, such as updating the findings of the report, and interviewing witnesses. Nothing prohibits him from taking such actions, and doing so would at least rob Chinese diplomats of the opportunity to brag – as they do in the halls of the Palais des Nations – about having shut down discussion about their grotesque abuses.
Second, Turk could reallocate a resource over which he has a great deal of control: time. He should spend as much time with the victims and survivors of Beijing’s abuses as he has spent with the perpetrators. Not only should he hear their horror stories, but he should be seen to have met with them. Beijing is known for threatening officials not to meet people or attend events representing ideas it does not like, often labeling them anti-China or “terrorists.” Too many governments take this threat seriously, and the result is to further disempower people with legitimate positions on human rights – particularly victims. 
Third, Turk should set out ambitious agendas to address alleged Chinese government crimes against humanity, including articulating legal pathways to accountability. But he should also directly address the concerns repeatedly set out by U.N. human rights experts, known as “special procedures,” who have for six years sounded alarms about Beijing’s non-compliance with and manipulation of its obligations under international human rights law. They have asked for the kind of help leadership requires: a special session at the HRC on China, the appointment of an expert specifically on China, greater attention to Beijing’s growing hostility toward U.N. human rights mechanisms.
Finally, Turk can help deny Beijing with “blue washing” its reputation through U.N. human rights reviews. Chinese diplomats shrilly insist there are no human rights abuses in the country. The best response to this position? Relentless public confrontation using facts and specifics: that allegations of crimes against humanity have also come from U.N. experts on arbitrary detention. That Beijing’s new “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law,” which is diametrically opposed to the government’s international obligations against discrimination, is another profound threat to the future of Tibetans, Uyghurs, and so many other groups already at risk of state-sponsored identity erasure. Nearly all 300 of the human rights lawyers detained, disbarred, or disappeared across China in 2015 have been unable to resume their essential – and legally protected – work. 
Turk has a unique opportunity – he knows the job, the institution, the geopolitics, and now has four full years to put that knowledge to good use. He is demonstrably comfortable challenging some permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, particularly Russia and the United States. His office has demonstrated its capacity to document Beijing’s human rights crimes; other U.N. human rights bodies regularly provide strong evidence of other abuses. He needs to understand the risks it takes for victims from China to reach out to his office, and how unique a responsibility he has speaking with them and on their behalf. 
The only outstanding question: will he put his new term to use in service of victims and survivors of Beijing’s abuses, and of accountability? That would be an outstanding legacy. Without such leadership the United Nations will become progressively less relevant on human rights – exactly the outcome several powerful states would like to see.

articles.title: Why Did China Sanction 2 High-Tech Institutions in Poland?
articles.full_text:
Beijing has offered no explanation for why these particular Polish entities were selected, but several recent developments are worth noting.
The main building of the Wrocław University of Science and Technology.
China has imposed sanctions on two Polish entities linked to the country’s defense and high-tech sectors. The move comes in response to the European Union’s 21st sanctions package against Russia. The latest EU measures targeted several companies from China and Hong Kong that are accused of supplying Moscow with technologies and components used in Russia’s war against Ukraine.
One of the Polish entities placed on China’s export control list is Wrocław University of Science and Technology (WUST), one of Poland’s leading technical universities with recognized expertise in satellite technologies, and space-related research. The other is Vigo Photonics, a high-tech manufacturer supplying components for the Polish Armed Forces as well as the Military University of Technology, Poland’s premier institution for military engineering.
This is not Beijing’s first move of this kind. In April, China’s Ministry of Commerce added seven European entities to its export control list in response to European measures targeting Chinese companies.
Responding to questions from the Polish Press Agency on July 27, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian emphasized that the decision was “a response to the EU’s erroneous move of listing and sanctioning Chinese companies” and stressed that “the measures do not target any specific country.”
Beijing’s decision to sanction WUST is particularly striking. The university participates in EU-funded projects on military drones and battlefield artificial intelligence. At the same time, it has been engaged in joint semiconductor research with Chinese universities.
“Wrocław University of Science and Technology is a poli-technical school with tradition and impact for regional and domestic Polish industry,” Krzysztof Karwowski, a researcher at the SGH Warsaw School of Economics, told The Diplomat.
“It is a leader primarily in advanced photonics and is the longest-established research center in this field in Poland, creates a number of engineering partnerships in Europe, and is the core of the Polish space industry: microsatellites and satellite optics for security.”
As for the implications of China’s move, Karwowski said it was “difficult to assess” at this point – “we will know them in the coming weeks.” 
He pointed out that WUST and Shanghai Jiao Tong University sealed a “partnership in the field of design and research on semiconductors” last year. “Given China’s activity at Polish academia, WUST may re-prioritize its collaborations in Asia, of which it has a number, to universities in India, Japan, or Korea,” Karwowski predicted.
The university’s inclusion on the sanctions list is puzzling, given its close scientific cooperation with Chinese institutions.
The other sanctioned entity, Vigo Photonics, specializes in manufacturing infrared detectors, building on research developed in cooperation with institutions such as the Military University of Technology. The company’s products are used across the energy, medical, railway, and defense sectors.
For the Polish Armed Forces, Vigo supplies infrared detectors used in unmanned aerial vehicles, precision-guided munitions, and self-guided weapons. Its components are also integrated into observation and targeting systems installed on armored vehicles and air-defense systems acquired by the Polish military.
Interestingly, the company itself had anticipated the possibility of Chinese restrictions. According to Vigo’s public statement: 
Aware of this risk, the company has for several years sourced these substrates primarily from suppliers in Japan and Europe, capable of covering its full demand. The company also maintains inventory sufficient for more than one year of production, ensuring continuity in manufacturing infrared detectors and modules.
Importantly, inclusion on China’s export control list does not automatically prohibit all trade. Under Chinese regulations, entities such as Vigo Photonics and Wrocław University of Science and Technology may still receive dual-use goods from China, provided exporters obtain the appropriate government license. In practice, this means Beijing retains discretion over future deliveries rather than imposing an outright embargo.
Beijing has offered no explanation for why these particular Polish entities were selected. While it is tempting to construct a broader geopolitical narrative, several recent developments are worth noting.
First, WUST is located only around 20 kilometers from the site of the recently announced Polish-Taiwanese Foxconn investment. Just weeks ago, Polish and Taiwanese officials unveiled plans for Taiwan to help revive two major industrial projects in Poland: an electric vehicle factory originally expected to be developed with Chinese partners, and a semiconductor project left behind after Intel abandoned its investment near Wrocław.
Second, the sanctions coincide with Poland’s growing role in Europe’s space sector. Two weeks ago, the European Space Agency announced that a new ESA Center for Civil Security and Resilience will be established in Warsaw, supporting the development of European capabilities in strategically important fields. Space technologies remain one of the fastest-growing arenas of geopolitical competition between China and Western countries, and as Karwowski noted, WUST is central to Poland’s space program.
Third, Beijing may also be responding to Poland’s increasingly visible political engagement with Taiwan. Earlier this month, former Polish Prime Minister Beata Szydło led a delegation of Members of the European Parliament from the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) group to Taiwan, where they met President Lai Ching-te and senior representatives of Taiwan’s government and business community.
In crafting its latest sanctions, China may have chosen Polish institutions that are important enough to send a political message, but not so important that they would seriously damage scientific or business cooperation. In this sense, the sanctions appear to be more of a political signal than an attempt to cause major economic harm.

articles.title: The ‘Poisonous Heart’: Australia’s Most Secretive Base Draws New Scrutiny
articles.full_text:
The largest U.S. spy facility in the region attracted a massive protest action amid rising concerns about the Australia-U.S. alliance.
Protesters demand the closure of Pine Gap during a march to the base, July 20, 2026.
“In 1962, they took my grandfather, the Americans,” said Arrerente Elder Aunty Felicity while standing outside of Pine Gap, the largest U.S. spy base in Australia. 
She handed a printed letter to the Australian Federal Police Inspector Ken Napier at the gates of Pine Gap. 
Three generations of the Hayes family, the traditional owners of Kuyunba, stood next to the land occupied for 60 years by the largest Australia-U.S. joint defense facility in Australia.
Established in 1966, without the consent of traditional owners, the Pine Gap signals intelligence facility sits roughly 15 kilometers from Alice Springs. The access road leading to the base is lined with ominous signs warning, “NO THROUGH ROAD, GO BACK.” 
Percolated by the hum of drones overhead, the perimeter has all the markings of a spy base: high impenetrable gates marked by the strategic placement of surveillance apparatus. Access to sacred sites has been restricted for decades, hemmed in by Pine Gap’s edges. 
And on July 20, Aunty Felicity was joined by hundreds of activists to challenge the continued existence of the U.S. spy facility. Anti-militarist activists, academics and Traditional Owners traveled across the country, some from as far as 2,000km away, to reach the desert in the heart of Australia. It was the largest protest against Pine Gap since 1987, where some 300 people were arrested. 
AFP inspector Ken Napier greeted the Hayes family as they walked up to the gate to deliver the letter.  “Welcome,” he said.
Wyonna Hayes, the daughter of Aunty Felicity, looked angry as she responded, “You’re welcome to my country.”
Aunty Felicity delivered a speech, asking for the land, the Kuyunba, to be returned to the traditional owners. 
Many of Pine Gap’s custodians, including Aunty Felicity herself, live just a few kilometers away at Irrkerlantye, also known as White Gate, in conditions that stand in glaring contrast to the base’s heavily resourced compound.
The White Gate community lacks basic services that much of Australia takes for granted: water is trucked in, power comes from a small set of solar panels, and there is no sewerage. 
“We want people to support us to close down Pine Gap,” Aunty Felicity said, standing beside her sister Wyona, and daughter Jaquita. 
“We want them to know it’s a sacred site.” 
But she is also concerned about people she has never met. Among her requests is compensation for families in Gaza who have lost relatives in a war she said the base has helped enable. 
“We don’t want to be feeling guilty all the time,” she said, “when bad things are happening overseas to the little ones.”
“We’re not the ones controlling that facility,” she continued, “but we feel guilty that it’s coming from our land.” 
The police had set up two checkpoints before the march had even reached the base: one several kilometers out on the highway to check identification, and a second closer to the gate to stop the march on foot. 
The protesters were undeterred. Chanting and banging on drums they cried, “Close Pine Gap,” “Shut it down,” and “Always was, always will be Aboriginal land.”
Later that morning, a lone protester, Aahana Nag, locked herself to the steering wheel of a car blocking the base’s only access road, closing it for just over an hour before her arrest.
“The United States has displaced the custodians of these lands and has built an intelligence facility that provides critical intelligence for their illegal military operations,” Nag said afterwards. 
“This base is material proof of the federal government’s investment in U.S. wars that do not serve us.”
The action was the climax of a three-day convergence devoted to the history of U.S. militarism in the Northern Territory, organized by activist groups Mparntwe for Falastin and the Anti-Militarism Action Network. With over 600 in attendance, it focused on the history of Pine Gap and the resistance to it.
Convergence organizer Jorgen Doyle attributed the action’s success to a growing unease in Australia over the U.S. alliance. 
“It’s a really compelling geopolitical moment,” he said, “to contest Pine Gap and everything that it represents.” 
“Northern Australia is the top overseas location for US Air Force and Navy construction spending,” he added, referring to a report in Reuters published in 2024. According to the report, more than $300 million was set aside over several years under U.S. congressional defense authorizations to fund the construction. 
According to Dr. Richard Tanter, Pine Gap is as secretive as it is misunderstood. 
Widely considered Australia’s leading expert on Pine Gap, Tanter is a senior research associate at the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability, where he has tracked the base’s expansion for over a decade, building on research alongside the late Des Ball and fellow researcher Bill Robinson. 
He told the convergence that the government’s habit of describing Pine Gap as a single facility is misleading.
articles.summary: The largest U.S. spy facility in the region attracted a massive protest action amid rising concerns about the Australia-U.S. alliance.

articles.title: Christianity in China: Testing Religious Freedom
articles.full_text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Paul H. B. Chang – associate professor in the Department of Religious Studies at the University of California at Riverside and author of “The Spiritual Person: An Intellectual Biography of Watchman Nee” (Oxford 2026) – is the 519th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
Identify the top three trends of Christianity in China.
I would say that probably the top three trends are the continued growth and vibrancy of Christianity in China, the increasing scrutiny and pressure placed on Christian organizations and their activities by the CCP [Chinese Community Party], and Chinese Christians’ theological and practical responses to their changing political and social environments. 
Although I use the word Christian, here and for the rest of the interview I am really speaking primarily of Protestants. In China, both legally and linguistically, Protestants and Catholics operate almost as two separate religions. Practically speaking, there is significant interaction and overlap but an expert on Chinese Catholicism would be better placed to talk about how much of this interview applies to Chinese Catholic circles. 
I also want to clarify that my work mostly centers on what one might consider more abstract, strictly theological trends. Thus, the top three trends I personally find most interesting relate to Chinese Christian perspectives on the nature and role of the church, differing doctrines on salvation, and contrasting perspectives on human nature. 
As far as the church is concerned, like all Christians, Chinese Christians have a longstanding interest in balancing the needs of the local and the universal church. They have thought a lot about how authority and administration can be both locally responsive and universally coherent. There is also a related, ongoing debate among Chinese Christians about how much the church should engage with secular society, both in terms of the government and in terms of wider cultural trends. 
Then, in terms of salvation, I think Chinese Christians once again have their own interesting, internal debate that roughly corresponds to theological trends outside of China. Whereas Reformed Christians have focused on more forensic, systematic perspectives on salvation, Watchman Nee is representative of an alternative train of thought that sees salvation as something more organic, seated in the union between the human and the divine.
This leads into my third perspective – that is, contrasting perspectives on human nature. Once again, I see the two main intellectual options as being something like a Reformed tradition, where the divine and human are more strictly delineated and kept apart, and a more mystical perspective, which sees some sort of ontological union as not only as possible but fundamental. 
Examine Western misconceptions about Chinese Christians.
Especially for Chinese Christians who follow or are influenced by Watchman Nee, their primary concern is not with political repression nor with asking for political support from outside China. Their theological mission is largely orthogonal to political changes and continues whether there is widespread support or disapprobation. And yet, they are very interested in communicating their universal vision with the world. 
They have a message for Western Christianity, indeed, for the Western secular world at large – namely that Jesus is coming and that sadly, most Christians and churches have not met his standard and may be found lacking on Jesus’s return. Few Westerners have heard their teaching that human beings should prepare for the end by being united in pure, local churches. In such local congregations, individual members can practice self-denial in self-sacrificing love for one another. This stands in stark contrast to this modern age of self-indulgence and self-promotion, which, they would argue, brings only misery.
Describe the scope of Watchman Nee’s faith and intellectual leadership beyond China.
Nee’s message is quite legible and even attractive to Westerners, especially to those of an evangelical Christian heritage. During the later years of his imprisonment, especially during the 1960s and 1970s, he became something of a cause célèbre among readers throughout the world, as a living example of a Christian suffering for his faith. He is quite readable in Chinese and he wrote a few key books in eloquent English as well, such as “The Normal Christian Life.” His writings have sold millions of copies and have been translated into dozens of languages. 
Furthermore, his influence shows no sign of slowing down, even more than 50 years after his death. In fact, given his popularity in non-Western Christian circles, such as in Africa and Latin America, it is quite possible that he has more readers than ever in 2026. 
All of this means that Watchman Nee belongs to a very select group of Chinese thinkers whose ideas and writings have spread beyond China and the Sinosphere and can truly be considered part of a global intellectual conversation. This small circle includes figures such as Confucius, Lao Zi, and Mao Zedong. Like them, Nee’s influence is not only broad but also deep. While many have casually read or appreciated Nee’s work, for some people, it has become a central moral compass and a guide to their human lives. In thousands of congregations on all six continents, there are hundreds of thousands of avid readers of Nee’s work who actively promote his perspectives on the Bible and on the ideal shape of Christian life. 
In these arenas, Nee’s clear message is that traditional or nominal Christianity alone cannot accomplish God’s goal and purpose for humanity. What God seeks is not adherents who donate money, defend orthodox doctrines, or perform certain rituals faithfully, but true worshippers whose entire lives come out of a radical root of self-denial. This self-denial is neither asceticism nor harsh self-treatment, but the spontaneous forgetting of the self that comes out of a deep love for Christ and the church. 
Explain the significance of recognition by the 111th (2009-2011) and 113th (2013-2015) U.S. Congress of Watchman Nee’s contributions to Christian thought in China.  
In both the 111th and 113th U.S. Congress, Watchman Nee was formally recognized by members of the United States Congress. These are more formal, political manifestations of the larger grassroots support Nee has generally received over the decades. In Christian circles, Nee has been lauded by influential figures across the Protestant spectrum ranging from Jerry Falwell and Carl Henry to Kenneth Hagin and Benny Hinn. Nee has even found followers in popular culture, including Bono and other members of the Irish rock band, U2, who seriously considered giving up their career in popular music because of Nee’s teachings on the self. 
All of these point to the rather undeniable facts that I believe are tacitly acknowledged even within Chinese government circles, namely that Watchman Nee, and his most significant follower Witness Lee, are important figures of world history. As the 113th U.S. Congress statement pointed out, it is ironic that with China’s growing presence on the global stage, some of its greatest thinkers cannot even be legally read within its own borders and their influence abroad cannot be openly acknowledged.
Assess the impact of Watchman Nee’s Christian thought on religious freedom in China-U.S. people-to-people relations.  
Nee’s relationship with religious freedom is interesting. He held to a core set of non-negotiable beliefs for which he was willing to suffering imprisonment and even martyrdom, like many Christians before him. Besides these core, rather theological values, he was willing to compromise and work with the government quite a lot. He felt that obedience to human authority as an extension of God’s authority was a key Christian virtue, and while he was imprisoned, he seems to have behaved himself as an exemplary inmate, except in his unwillingness to recant his faith. 
The people-to-people relationships between Nee’s followers within and outside of China are a key test case for the limits and possibilities for religious speech in civic and political spaces. Individual followers of Nee may and do hold a range of political opinions. Nevertheless, as a corporate body – that is, as the church – they are categorically opposed to direct involvement in politics, except to obey any explicit commands that do not contradict the gospel. It is hard to imagine a more politically quietist Protestant group. 
And yet, despite their quiescent nature, the very fact of their constituting a moral community does create an independent authority within the larger body politic. I suppose that from a completely paranoid perspective, even a completely subservient church may seem to pose a threat because of its independent existence. Still, members of congregations that follow Nee have struck me as model citizens wherever I have met them, whether in the U.S. or China. They tend to be scrupulously honest in their personal and professional lives and see a law-abiding, respectful attitude toward government as a meaningful part of their personal piety and Christian witness.

articles.title: The Cockroach Uprising: How the CJP Protest Exposed India’s Broken Institutions
articles.full_text:
Journalist and author Snigdhendu Bhattacharya joins host Tushar Shetty to examine what the Cockroach Janata Party protests reveal about the erosion of India’s democratic institutions.
Independent journalist and author Snigdhendu Bhattacharya joins host Tushar Shetty to examine what the Cockroach Janata Party protests reveal about the erosion of India’s democratic institutions. They discuss the satirical origins of the movement and the exam-leak grievances that fueled it, Sonam Wangchuk’s hunger strike and the government’s effort to brand the protesters as foreign funded, and the forcible removal of Wangchuk and the police crackdown of July 20. 
They also cover the sidelining of Parliament and the collapse of the opposition as a channel for dissent, the Election Commission’s loss of credibility after the disputed electoral roll revision in West Bengal, and the retreat of the judiciary and the mainstream press as independent checks on power. 
Bhattacharya argues that the movement grew as fast as it did precisely because every institutional avenue for grievance had already been hollowed out, leaving a frustrated generation with nowhere left to turn. 
This conversation was recorded on July 24, 2026, the day before Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned.
For more in-depth analysis on South Asia, subscribe to the Beyond the Indus podcast on Spotify or Apple Podcasts, or follow us on YouTube for video episodes.

articles.title: America’s Changing Policy on Afghanistan
articles.full_text:
Washington has moved from an emphasis on human rights to “selective” contacts driven by specific cases. That’s a win for the Taliban.
Since the haphazard and hasty withdrawal of U.S. and allied forces from Afghanistan in the summer of 2021, Washington has not recognized the Taliban – or any other group – as the legitimate government in Afghanistan. Washington asserts that it advocates for an inclusive government that respects human rights, including those of women and minorities. 
Since August 31, 2021, the U.S. embassy in Afghanistan has suspended its operations, and the Afghanistan Affairs Unit (AAU) in Qatar serves as the U.S. diplomatic mission for Afghanistan. Despite this, there have been selective contacts between U.S. officials and the Taliban over the past five years, primarily concerning counterterrorism, the release of prisoners, and the evacuation of U.S. citizens from Afghanistan.
The United States claims that it maintains contact with the Taliban only for specific cases. Ambassador Gregory D. LoGerfo, the U.S. State Department’s coordinator for counterterrorism, said last week that “with respect to the Taliban, we engage them selectively when it’s in the U.S. interest with respect to very discrete security issues.” 
In response, the Taliban’s ambassador to Doha, Suhail Shaheen, told TOLOnews that “Afghanistan no longer poses a threat to any country,” and that the Taliban government has “worked to combat destabilizing groups.” Shaheen added, “As is clear to everyone, our country needs reconstruction, economic development, and cooperation in various sectors. Therefore, taking these interests into account and in light of our principles, we want to establish and maintain relations with other countries. This is the principled framework of our policy.” 
Even “selective” contacts with the United States are significant for the Taliban. The Trump administration has reversed the U.S. foreign assistance and immigration policy toward Afghanistan. Under the Biden administration, the United States disbursed over $3.8 billion for development and humanitarian assistance in Afghanistan after October 2021. However, the Trump administration has terminated all foreign assistance to Afghanistan starting in mid-2025 despite the ongoing humanitarian crisis in the country. 
Besides this, President Donald Trump halted programs to resettled Afghans who worked on behalf of the U.S. in Afghanistan during its so-called war on terror in the country. From August 2021 to mid-2025, over 190,000 Afghan nationals were resettled in the United States. Shortly after taking office for his second term, Trump ended these facilities and shut the U.S. State Department’s Office of the Coordinator for Afghan Relocation Efforts (CARE). The current administration also suspended the processing of all visas to Afghan nationals, including Special Immigrant Visas (SIVs).
For the United States, Afghanistan is a matter of the past. Washington often shows reluctance to discuss the Afghanistan war, mirroring the political and cultural avoidance that followed the U.S. war on Vietnam between 1955 and 1975. Just like in Vietnam, Washington failed to meet its objective in Afghanistan. The Taliban returned to power after the United States had fought against the group for almost two decades. That was quickly followed by a haphazard U.S. withdrawal, which indeed was a face-saving act. 
Afghanistan seems to have lost its place in public discourse and as a foreign policy priority in the U.S. after its withdrawal from the country. Perhaps that is why the country does not appear in Washington’s 2025 National Security Strategy or the 2026 National Defense Strategy. 
One of the few areas of contact between Washington and the Taliban are talks over prisoner swaps. In January 2025, during the last hours of the Biden administration, the Taliban released two American citizens, George Gelzmann and Mahmood Habibi, in exchange for an Afghan national. The swap was the result of several rounds of negotiations spanning over two years under the mediation of Qatar. Since then, several other U.S. citizens detained in Afghanistan have been released by the Taliban government. Even though these negotiations are merely for the release of U.S. citizens, for the Taliban, they present an opportunity to sit across the table with U.S. officials. The United States calls it an abhorrent practice of “hostage diplomacy,” but for the de facto rulers of Afghanistan it is a practical approach to showcase their rule over the country.
Another area of focus for the United States – at least in rhetoric – is the issue of human rights, particularly the rights of women in Afghanistan under Taliban rule. At the time of the U.S. invasion of Afghanistan in October 2001, Washington used the Taliban’s gender-based repression as part of its argument for invading the country. In this regard, Laura Bush, the first lady, in a radio address argued that “the fight against terrorism is also a fight for the rights of women.” 
However, in the 2020 Doha Process talks between the U.S. and the Taliban, there was no mention of the rights of women and girls. Moreover, the Trump administration is criticized for sidelining Afghan women in its contacts with the Taliban, which do not touch on rights issues. That leaves women and girls in Afghanistan in the lurch.
For Washington, it might be “selective,” issue-based diplomacy, but for the Taliban, it is a significant boost. Each round of negotiations gives a clear message to the international community that it is the Taliban’s de facto government that rules Afghanistan, despite sanctions and international pressure for almost five years. With or without recognition, it is the Taliban that get to sit at the table to negotiate with foreign officials. 
The Taliban with a slow and steady approach have extended their rule in the country without bowing to pressure from the international community. In fact, that pressure seems to have receded over time. The Taliban regime managed to get their first diplomatic recognition last year from none other than their erstwhile enemy, Russia, and have cozied up to another former enemy, India, over the past two years.

For the United States, Afghanistan is a matter of the past. Washington often shows reluctance to discuss the Afghanistan war, mirroring the political and cultural avoidance that followed the U.S. war on Vietnam between 1955 and 1975. Just like in Vietnam, Washington failed to meet its objective in Afghanistan. The Taliban returned to power after the United States had fought against the group for almost two decades. That was quickly followed by a haphazard U.S. withdrawal, which indeed was a face-saving act. 
Afghanistan seems to have lost its place in public discourse and as a foreign policy priority in the U.S. after its withdrawal from the country. Perhaps that is why the country does not appear in Washington’s 2025 National Security Strategy or the 2026 National Defense Strategy. 
One of the few areas of contact between Washington and the Taliban are talks over prisoner swaps. In January 2025, during the last hours of the Biden administration, the Taliban released two American citizens, George Gelzmann and Mahmood Habibi, in exchange for an Afghan national. The swap was the result of several rounds of negotiations spanning over two years under the mediation of Qatar. Since then, several other U.S. citizens detained in Afghanistan have been released by the Taliban government. Even though these negotiations are merely for the release of U.S. citizens, for the Taliban, they present an opportunity to sit across the table with U.S. officials. The United States calls it an abhorrent practice of “hostage diplomacy,” but for the de facto rulers of Afghanistan it is a practical approach to showcase their rule over the country.
Another area of focus for the United States – at least in rhetoric – is the issue of human rights, particularly the rights of women in Afghanistan under Taliban rule. At the time of the U.S. invasion of Afghanistan in October 2001, Washington used the Taliban’s gender-based repression as part of its argument for invading the country. In this regard, Laura Bush, the first lady, in a radio address argued that “the fight against terrorism is also a fight for the rights of women.” 
However, in the 2020 Doha Process talks between the U.S. and the Taliban, there was no mention of the rights of women and girls. Moreover, the Trump administration is criticized for sidelining Afghan women in its contacts with the Taliban, which do not touch on rights issues. That leaves women and girls in Afghanistan in the lurch.
For Washington, it might be “selective,” issue-based diplomacy, but for the Taliban, it is a significant boost. Each round of negotiations gives a clear message to the international community that it is the Taliban’s de facto government that rules Afghanistan, despite sanctions and international pressure for almost five years. With or without recognition, it is the Taliban that get to sit at the table to negotiate with foreign officials. 
The Taliban with a slow and steady approach have extended their rule in the country without bowing to pressure from the international community. In fact, that pressure seems to have receded over time. The Taliban regime managed to get their first diplomatic recognition last year from none other than their erstwhile enemy, Russia, and have cozied up to another former enemy, India, over the past two years.
Since the haphazard and hasty withdrawal of U.S. and allied forces from Afghanistan in the summer of 2021, Washington has not recognized the Taliban – or any other group – as the legitimate government in Afghanistan. Washington asserts that it advocates for an inclusive government that respects human rights, including those of women and minorities. 
Since August 31, 2021, the U.S. embassy in Afghanistan has suspended its operations, and the Afghanistan Affairs Unit (AAU) in Qatar serves as the U.S. diplomatic mission for Afghanistan. Despite this, there have been selective contacts between U.S. officials and the Taliban over the past five years, primarily concerning counterterrorism, the release of prisoners, and the evacuation of U.S. citizens from Afghanistan.
Muhammad Murad is a Ph.D. Political Science Candidate at the University of Bonn, Germany.
articles.summary: Washington has moved from an emphasis on human rights to “selective” contacts driven by specific cases. That's a win for the Taliban.

articles.title: Sri Lanka’s Tariff Concession May Carry a Diplomatic Cost With China
articles.full_text:
To avoid higher US tariffs, Sri Lanka is having to act as if allegations of forced labor against China, a country with a high level of mechanization, are credible.
An aerial view of Sri Lanka’s Colombo port as seen from the Lotus Tower.
Imagine that you have two powerful friends you cannot afford to lose. One of them often threatens to punish you unless you publicly denounce the other for something you know the other didn’t do. But you comply because you depend on that friend. But now the other friend is watching, and you’re left hoping they will still take your calls.
This is the position Sri Lanka often finds itself in with regard to the United States and China.
In early July, Sri Lanka issued a gazette to ban the import of goods produced using forced labor. The gazette says that the government has imposed a blanket ban on importing any goods that were made, mined, or produced, wholly or even partially, using forced labor.
The government will also publish a list of high-risk goods, companies, and countries, as per findings of the International Labor Organization (ILO). If an importer brings in products from one of those flagged sources, they have to provide evidence that the goods were not made using forced labor. The Director General of Customs will enforce this directive.
On paper, this looks like a worthy initiative; no one supports forced labor. But in practice, this was the United States making Sri Lanka take part in a game it doesn’t want to play. In June, Washington announced that countries that fail to prohibit “forced labor imports” would face heavy tariffs. Sri Lanka sends a quarter of its exports to the American market, and could not afford to be placed in the punishment bracket.
By adopting the ban, Sri Lanka secured the lower 10 percent tariff rate. Sri Lanka is among 17 economies (also including Canada, India, Mexico, and the U.K.) that were taxed 10 percent because they have “made commitments to adopt, and effectively enforce, forced labor import prohibitions.” A 12.5 percent rate was applied to countries that have, according to Washington, failed to adopt a formal forced-labor import prohibition.
Sri Lankan businesses and politicians have reacted positively to the 10 percent tariff as they believe it puts them in an equal or better position than their key competitors. The Joint Apparel Association Forum (JAAF), which represents the apparel industry in the country, said that the industry is competitive and even a narrow percentage point difference in tariffs could mean the “difference between winning and losing an order to a rival sourcing destination.” This was a sentiment shared by the Exporters Association of Sri Lanka (EASL) and former minister of finance, as well as foreign affairs, Ravi Karunanayake.
While Sri Lanka was only subjected to an additional duty of 10 percent, there was uncertainty between the announcement of possible tariffs in early June and the date that tariffs were announced — a period of almost two months. Sources from the apparel sector told The Diplomat that there were serious concerns about lost orders and job losses during those two months.
As Karunanayake pointed out, there is no evidence to suggest that Sri Lanka imports anything from destinations that use forced labor. Trump has used tariffs as a cornerstone of his foreign policy and uses them to negotiate trade deals around the globe. Countries like Sri Lanka that depend heavily on exports to the United States are especially vulnerable to such moves.

Therefore, Sri Lanka has to adopt an attitude of deference to the U.S. and carries out performative actions, such as issuing gazettes banning the import of goods produced using forced labor.
But what does the U.S. mean by goods made using forced labor? In the past few decades, China has become the leading trade partner of almost all countries and the U.S. has been using tariffs to dissuade the world from trading with China. Its not surprising that Washington has singled out China as a country that uses forced labor, which it alleges gives China an unfair advantage over the United States.

A few years ago, the BBC stated that close to half a million workers were coerced into picking cotton in Xinjiang. This often-repeated cotton-picking headline is at odds with the data.
In the 1980s and the 1990s, China relied heavily on its vast and educated workforce to produce goods cheaply. But that has not been the case for at least 10-15 years. Chinese labor is no longer cheap. It is also a highly mechanized country. In 2024, 542,000 industrial robots were installed worldwide, with China deploying 54 percent of them. Xinjiang is no exception to mechanization. Data from China shows that over 90 percent of Xinjiang’s cotton was machine-picked, up from 5 percent in 1990. articles.title: What Ails India’s Education Sector
articles.full_text:
What India needs is deep systemic changes to its education system, economy, and more generally, the life that it offers its youth.
Indian medical students writing an exam, March 2022.
On July 25, student protests in India, led by the satirical Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), achieved their demand of forcing Dharmendra Pradhan, the minister of education in the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government, to resign.
The genesis of the protests, which had been ongoing for several weeks, was the leakage of question papers of the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (Undergraduate), otherwise known as the NEET (UG), held on May 3. The exam was canceled and a re-exam was held on June 21.
This caused enormous distress to students and parents, who had much at stake in clearing the exams and beginning the admissions process. At least a dozen students committed suicide after the test was canceled.
In India, students spend years preparing for exams and attending coaching classes in order to have a shot at getting into a number of competitive professions with limited seats. These include medicine, law, management, the civil service, and even the police force, as shown in the recent award-winning Indian film “Homebound.” This is quite different from many Western countries, many of which have a more flexible labor market and allow entry into a profession at any point in life, so long as one completes the proper degree and licensing. It is not unheard of for someone to attend law school or medical school in their 40s.
For many in India, especially the poorer sections of society or members of Dalit and backward castes, attaining success after clearing such an exam is their primary shot at upward mobility. Another recent Indian movie, “12th Fail,” became a sleeper hit by reflecting the aspirations of millions by showing how an individual, through hard work, ended up clearing the civil service exam after nearly a decade of grinding through college and coaching classes. Once appointed to the civil service, an individual with such a coveted government job is considered set for life, thus bringing honor and wealth to his or her family, not to mention better marriage prospects for relatives.
But for every successful candidate, there are many more unsuccessful ones. And those who fail to clear exams — or never even take them, due to cancellations — often become despondent, having lost years of their lives. Up to 25,000 students in India committed suicide between 2014 and 2024.
While at its core, the cancellation of the NEET exam in May was due to corruption — and the fight to get the education minister to resign was about holding someone responsible for the leak — this issue highlights larger problems and trends in India. If anything, the demands of the protesters were strangely narrow and seemed to miss the larger issue. A change in government is not the answer; what’s needed is a deep change in policy.
Even if there was no corruption and there were no exam leaks, even if there were a different government in Delhi, there would still be millions of young Indians toiling away at rote memorization during the best years of their lives, competing for a small number of seats. Many would still not get into the profession of their choice and many, driven by poverty or family pressure, would still commit suicide. For exams that are ostensibly supposed to fill professions and the civil services on the basis of merit, over half the seats are not filled through open competition, but through quotas for various caste and tribal groups. Over the course of the past few decades, the percentage of spots reserved for different caste groups has ballooned, with widespread demand even among upper castes for reservations so as not to lose out on their perceived share of seats.
India’s entire education system thus prepares individuals for a series of tests designed to restrict entry into professions that are defined by artificial scarcity. In the public sector, this artificial scarcity is a function of tight budgets and the need of many bureaucrats to maintain the prestige of their positions, which is enhanced by a limited number of appointments.
India faces a shortage of police officers, for example, with 153 police officers for 100,000 people in 2023, well below the United Nations recommended ratio of 222:100,000. Nineteen percent of the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) is currently unfilled. India’s diplomatic corps is notoriously underfilled. The world’s most populous country should not have so much difficulty finding people to staff its bureaucracy.
This issue has also manifested in the private sector. A country as large as India needs more doctors, lawyers, and judges as well, but entrance into the medical and legal professions is similarly constrained by the bottleneck of exams, accreditation, and not enough staff for specialized training. Thus, a large number of medical students must compete for a smaller number of internships and specializations before practicing medicine. India’s doctor to people ratio is 1:811, whilst that of the United States is 1:313.
While the number of seats in many professions, such as the civil service and medicine, should be increased to match increased demand, and the nature of exams rethought, this is not enough. More people need more jobs across the board.
India’s education system, by and large, does not emphasize research, critical thinking, or learning how to learn, all of which are especially important in preparing individuals for an information economy and encouraging the growth of the private sector and entrepreneurialism. The education methodologies and outcomes that drive learning, economic growth, and participation in civil society, should be placed at the forefront of India’s education system.
The growth of industry and the private sector in general is important because they create many more high-paying jobs across industries than what the public sector can generate. This, in turn, would reduce the pressure on so many individuals to compete for a small number of stable and well-paying government jobs. An individual should not have to depend only on a government job to earn a decent livelihood. India’s private sector must expand, by necessity, to absorb its growing educated workforce, as it would be impossible for everyone to be a government employee.
The recent protests made a few, well-defined minimalist demands: resignation of a minister, and compensation for the families of those who committed suicide. But underlying their demands and contributing to their ferocity is wider frustration with the opportunities and options available to youth. And while these frustrations focused primarily on education and jobs, the mobilization of youth demonstrates an increased dissatisfaction and willingness to protest for causes close to their hearts. These are individuals who have higher expectations for their lives, having seen how the rest of the world lives, studies, plays, and works on their smartphones.
Judging by the thoughts and words — replete with memes, profanity, sarcasm, humor, and references to pop culture — expressed by many of the young protesters, India is at the threshold of a 1960s-style generational revolt against authority and institutions, something that will have profound social and political implications in the years to come. articles.title: Uzbekistan Launches Its First Tax-Free Crypto Mining Zone
articles.full_text:
Uzbekistan wants to reap the economic benefits of cryptocurrency, while keeping the industry regulated.
On July 8, Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Justice approved a regulation governing registration and operations of the residents of the Besqala Mining Valley. Prospectors here won’t be mining for gold, uranium, or copper – they are mining cryptocurrency.
Developed by the National Agency for Prospective Projects (NAPP), the new regulation is in accordance with the presidential resolution from April 17 to establish the first-of-its-kind special crypto mining zone in the Republic of Karakalpakstan, covering its whole territory. Within Besqala, incomes from crypto mining are exempted from taxes until 2035. That creates an incentivizing environment for large mining operators, although it’s notable that only locally registered legal entities can become Besqala residents.
Uzbekistan’s position on cryptocurrency is somewhere in between full prohibition and unrestricted permission. The state allows crypto activities to exist, but they must be traceable and financially controllable. Initially, in 2018, Tashkent established a highly controlled approach toward cryptocurrencies. Various crypto activities, including mining, were recognized and regarded as an economic and technological opportunity, but within limits. From October 2018, crypto activities required state licensing, to be handled by the National Agency for Project Management under the president. Tashkent also granted certain perks for crypto activities, such as exemption from taxes and ordinary currency-control rules. Mining was not yet treated as an electricity or environmental threat. 
The 2022 reforms in the crypto field positioned the NAPP as a principal regulator responsible for licensing, registering, and even investigating foreign entities. Crypto mining itself became a corporate practice – only legal entities can mine – and was subject to Uzbekistan’s energy policy – mining must use electricity generated by solar stations. From 2023, crypto mining practices required a permit from the NAPP, not a license. The permits are issued for five years and are listed publicly by the NAPP. 
The 2023 amendments to Uzbekistan’s Criminal Code, which entered into force from January 2024, had implications for crypto regulations. Initially, violations in the crypto sphere, including in mining activities, might result in administrative punishments such as confiscation of equipment and a fine. Now, such violations lead to criminal liability. Covert (yashirin) mining can be criminal from its first occurrence. The law also legally defined “crypto asset” and “mining” and entered them into the country’s Criminal Code.
The introduction of Besqala Mining Valley represents more opportunities for the state to supervise crypto mining practices. This is important especially in relation to energy consumption, since mining requires a lot of it. In 2024 alone, 91 crypto mining farms were found to be engaging in electricity theft. In Besqala, crypto miners now have more liberalized electricity use: they can use many forms of renewable energy and hydrogen-generated electricity, while in other parts of Uzbekistan only solar electricity is allowed for mining. Apart from that, Besqala residents may connect to the national grid but have to pay twice as much as regular users. Concentrating mining operators in one geographic location makes the industry’s activities, including electricity use, more visible.
What is important is that the Besqala Mining Valley is not a separate industrial park, but covers all of Karakalpakstan, which is almost 40 percent of Uzbekistan’s total territory. This might make environmental monitoring hard. Questions such as electronic waste, water consumption, cooling, noise, heat discharge (except for the heat being reused for greenhouses – but this is not mandatory for mining operators), equipment disposal, or environmental-impact assessments are yet to be addressed. Crypto miners paying twice as much to use electricity from the national grid also does not guarantee that local households can avoid electricity shortages, especially in mid-summer when everyone wants to use air conditioning. 
Just between July 13 and 19 the People’s Receptions of the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan received 1,012 applications regarding power outages and 356 on repairing electrical facilities. In the first half of 2026, electricity losses reportedly amounted to 17.2 percent (equal to 4.8 billion kilowatt-hours). Current crypto mining regulations, however, do not establish maximum grid capacity for a single mining operator. 
The Besqala Mining Valley can also potentially contribute to the economy of Karakalpakstan, a region that is already geographically isolated and historically in need of additional measures to improve living conditions due to environmental challenges stemming from the drying Aral Sea. In August 2025, a presidential decree to accelerate the socio-economic development of Karakalpakstan was issued, including the idea of creating a mining zone among other measures. Due to tax privileges and more liberal energy use, large mining operators might relocate to Karakalpakstan. However, mining and other crypto-related activities create very few permanent positions. And if foreign miners come, they bring their own employees. The current regulations do not establish a minimum for locally created jobs. 
The success of the valley will be seen later, once it is visible how much new electricity generation crypto miners build (if they ever do), how much they draw from the existing grid, how it will affect the local households, and how much foreign currency revenue reaches Uzbek banks. For now, the launch of Besqala Mining Valley represents Tashkent’s effort to control a largely informal and difficult-to-regulate activity within a set territory and managed regulations.

What is important is that the Besqala Mining Valley is not a separate industrial park, but covers all of Karakalpakstan, which is almost 40 percent of Uzbekistan’s total territory. This might make environmental monitoring hard. Questions such as electronic waste, water consumption, cooling, noise, heat discharge (except for the heat being reused for greenhouses – but this is not mandatory for mining operators), equipment disposal, or environmental-impact assessments are yet to be addressed. Crypto miners paying twice as much to use electricity from the national grid also does not guarantee that local households can avoid electricity shortages, especially in mid-summer when everyone wants to use air conditioning. 
Just between July 13 and 19 the People’s Receptions of the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan received 1,012 applications regarding power outages and 356 on repairing electrical facilities. In the first half of 2026, electricity losses reportedly amounted to 17.2 percent (equal to 4.8 billion kilowatt-hours). Current crypto mining regulations, however, do not establish maximum grid capacity for a single mining operator. 
The Besqala Mining Valley can also potentially contribute to the economy of Karakalpakstan, a region that is already geographically isolated and historically in need of additional measures to improve living conditions due to environmental challenges stemming from the drying Aral Sea. In August 2025, a presidential decree to accelerate the socio-economic development of Karakalpakstan was issued, including the idea of creating a mining zone among other measures. Due to tax privileges and more liberal energy use, large mining operators might relocate to Karakalpakstan. However, mining and other crypto-related activities create very few permanent positions. And if foreign miners come, they bring their own employees. The current regulations do not establish a minimum for locally created jobs. 
The success of the valley will be seen later, once it is visible how much new electricity generation crypto miners build (if they ever do), how much they draw from the existing grid, how it will affect the local households, and how much foreign currency revenue reaches Uzbek banks. For now, the launch of Besqala Mining Valley represents Tashkent’s effort to control a largely informal and difficult-to-regulate activity within a set territory and managed regulations. 
On July 8, Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Justice approved a regulation governing registration and operations of the residents of the Besqala Mining Valley. Prospectors here won’t be mining for gold, uranium, or copper – they are mining cryptocurrency.
Developed by the National Agency for Prospective Projects (NAPP), the new regulation is in accordance with the presidential resolution from April 17 to establish the first-of-its-kind special crypto mining zone in the Republic of Karakalpakstan, covering its whole territory. Within Besqala, incomes from crypto mining are exempted from taxes until 2035. That creates an incentivizing environment for large mining operators, although it’s notable that only locally registered legal entities can become Besqala residents.
Niginakhon Saida is a doctoral research fellow at MALVA Center for the Study of War, Language, and Memory at JGU Mainz.
articles.summary: Uzbekistan wants to reap the economic benefits of cryptocurrency, while keeping the industry regulated.

articles.title: RIMPAC 2026 and the Future of Multinational Maritime Operations in the Indo-Pacific
articles.full_text:
This year’s iteration of the exercise reflects several important strategic concepts – and a focus on countering China’s navy.
Multinational ships sail in formation during Exercise Rim of the Pacific 2026 (RIMPAC 2026) in the Pacific Ocean, July 22, 2026.
The biennial Rim of the Pacific Exercise, or RIMPAC, is one of the most important military exercises in the Indo-Pacific. This year’s theme, “Partners: Integrated and Prepared,” highlights the central purpose of the U.S.-led exercise: strengthening collective defense and multinational operational coordination across the region. 
More specifically, RIMPAC is designed to integrate the operational mechanisms, command procedures, and military systems of the United States and its allies and partners. RIMPAC 2026, which started on June 24 and will conclude on July 31, reflects several important strategic concepts.
One of the most important features of this year’s RIMPAC is the emphasis on submarines and anti-submarine warfare aircraft. This reflects growing concern over the expanding carrier and undersea capabilities of the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN).
Since the previous RIMPAC in 2024, China’s aircraft carrier development and operations have drawn increasing international attention. In addition to conducting more frequent maritime exercises in the Western Pacific, China has also introduced new carrier-related aircraft, including newer variants of the J-15 and the J-35. The Liaoning has carried out repeated takeoff and landing training in the East China Sea and the Western Pacific. In 2025, China’s two-carrier operations beyond the First Island Chain and deeper into the Pacific further heightened regional concern over the PLAN’s carrier capabilities. These developments naturally make China’s carrier strike groups a major focus as participating countries seek to integrate and coordinate their operational capabilities during RIMPAC.
At present, the deployment of land-based anti-ship missiles remains an important tactic for the United States and its allies along the First Island Chain. This “using land to control the sea” approach is a practical way to counter the PLAN. However, when it comes to countering Chinese aircraft carriers, undersea attack remains one of the most effective options. Compared with engaging the PLAN through surface anti-ship or air-defense operations, submarines can provide a more survivable and effective means of threatening carrier strike groups.
How to integrate undersea forces for operations against PLAN carrier formations will therefore be one of the key areas of training for the United States and its partners in this year’s RIMPAC. Five submarines are reportedly taking part in RIMPAC 2026, compared to just three in RIMPAC 2024.
Learning From Recent U.S. Combat Experience
Another important aspect of this year’s exercise is the opportunity for participating countries to learn from recent U.S. operational experience, particularly in air defense, counter-drone operations, and responses to unmanned surface vessels in the Middle East.
For the 30 participating countries, RIMPAC is not only an opportunity to conduct joint exercises with the U.S. military and become familiar with one another’s doctrines and new equipment. It is also a platform for system integration and combined personnel training. This is one of the main reasons why countries continue to attach importance to participation in RIMPAC.
In recent years, however, U.S. forces have also accumulated valuable real-world experience in the Middle East. Recent operations have shown that traditional missile defense systems are facing new challenges. The most pressing aerial threat today is no longer limited to aircraft or missiles, but increasingly comes from large numbers of low-cost unmanned systems. This has forced air-defense systems to adapt to a changing threat environment.
The various drones and unmanned surface vessels encountered by U.S. forces in the Middle East provide lessons that are extremely valuable for other countries. These are precisely the kinds of battlefield experiences that participating states will seek to absorb from the United States during RIMPAC 2026.
RIMPAC also included a multinational live-fire sinking exercise, known as SINKEX. This year’s target vessels reportedly include the decommissioned amphibious assault ship Peleliu and the former Aegis cruiser Mobile Bay. Participating forces will conduct live-fire attacks from land, sea, and air, testing multinational strike coordination, weapons integration, and command-and-control capabilities. Before launching the strikes, participating countries will also have the opportunity to test maritime replenishment and joint logistical coordination.
The purpose of SINKEX is not only to allow participating personnel to experience the impact of live-fire operations. It also provides an opportunity to evaluate the effects of different weapons against real naval targets. The U.S. military can assess how many munitions are needed, where they should strike, and what kinds of damage are required to disable or sink different types of vessels.
This year’s target ships are especially noteworthy. A large amphibious assault ship and a 10,000-ton-class cruiser resemble, in general operational terms, the types of vessels the PLAN is now developing and deploying, including the Type 075 and Type 076 amphibious assault ships and the Type 055 large destroyer. In this sense, SINKEX is not only a weapons test. It is also a rehearsal for the kinds of maritime targets that allied forces may encounter in a future conflict.
Although Taiwan cannot send its military forces to participate in RIMPAC 2026, the exercise still deserves close attention. The core value of RIMPAC lies not only in the deployment of ships, aircraft, and troops, but also in the operation of command systems and the evolution of tactics. Whether Taiwan participates directly with forces is therefore not the only issue.
Taiwan’s own defense posture is centered primarily on island defense, which differs from RIMPAC’s emphasis on large-scale maritime and air operations across the open ocean. Given this difference in strategic objectives, Taiwan should pay particular attention to how participating countries integrate command systems, connect platforms, and coordinate operations across multiple domains.
Over the years, RIMPAC has provided the United States and its partners with a venue to test new operational concepts and tactics. These tactical innovations are worth studying closely. Taiwan may not face the same operational environment, and some aspects of large-scale multinational maritime operations may not directly apply to Taiwan’s defense needs. Nevertheless, by observing RIMPAC, Taiwan can better understand how emerging technologies are reshaping military operations.
For Taiwan, the most important lesson is not simply how many ships or aircraft participate in the exercise. Rather, it is how modern militaries integrate sensors, platforms, weapons, command networks, and allied forces into a coherent operational system. In this sense, RIMPAC remains an important window into the future of Indo-Pacific military cooperation – and a valuable reference point for Taiwan as it seeks to keep its own defense thinking up to date.

articles.title: Vietnam’s New AI Law and Its Strategic Implications
articles.full_text:
The country’s government is leading Southeast Asian efforts to regulate AI technologies, but its approach has several important shortcomings.
In March 2026, Vietnam began implementing its state-led, top-down AI law (Law 134/2025/QH15), one of the boldest moves to govern the juggernaut technology sector that any Southeast Asian government has made so far. For a country rapidly ramping up its high-tech ambitions, Vietnam’s AI regulatory measure aims to strengthen sovereign control over data flows, augment transparency, and mitigate against varying risks associated with AI. Moreover, it sets a benchmark for regulation within a region which has generally relied on voluntary compliance, as exemplified by ASEAN’s soft-law or guideline approach to AI governance.
But therein lies the rub. While Hanoi is forcefully implementing a standalone legal framework to assert control over information technology and strengthen state sovereignty, the Vietnamese government is ignoring the broader regulatory, socio-economic, and environmental implications. These include unintended consequences such as the sorts of economic dislocations and social disruptions that are inherent in such dynamic and historic transformations, although AI engenders change at exponential rates that could vastly widen already troubling societal inequalities.
Vietnam is not alone in its quest for enhanced digital sovereignty, and the stakes of the issue are high. The United States, China, Russia, and the European Union have long understood that key sectors – ranging from healthcare to energy and security – now operate on AI systems generally dominated by a handful of tech companies and the supply chains of critical minerals on which they rely. AI governance, therefore, increasingly encompasses the grand strategies of various global, national, and corporate stakeholders who are seeking to survive in a harshly competitive environment.
Vietnam’s new AI law creates a comprehensive legal framework, establishing a three-tier system of high, medium, and low categories of risk that align with differing levels of regulatory control. The higher the risk, the more government regulation. As a state-led approach, the law applies to both domestic and foreign entities conducting AI activities in Vietnam. While the law is still being implemented, it ideally aims to balance regulation with innovation and socio-economic development by allowing tech developers to test evolving AI models without strict penalties during a trial phase.
Although the law has its strengths, Vietnam’s AI law has several important shortcomings. First, the policy sits uneasily under ASEAN’s regional voluntary approach to AI regulation. Most troubling, it possibly creates a high-tech race to the bottom in the region, as venture capital often seeks jurisdictions with the least amount of regulation. Vietnam’s growing economy and quest for capital sits in a region increasingly shaped by ASEAN’s evolving governance architecture.
But the country’s AI law currently stands in contrast to ASEAN’s soft approach to AI regulation, at least for now. In February 2024, ASEAN issued its Guide on AI Governance and Ethics, which outlined principles of transparency, fairness, accountability, human-centricity, privacy, safety, and reliability. This framework was expanded in January 2025 to cover generative AI with nine areas of concern, including cybersecurity and content creation. ASEAN’s principle-based AI approach tends to mirror the EU’s emphasis on constructive engagement with the AI sector. By the end of 2026, ASEAN could potentially be moving to a legally binding approach under the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, which is expected to be signed later this year.
Vietnam’s AI law is also notable for what is omitted from regulation, such as the questions of how to manage environmental degradation and natural resource allocation. This omission is significant because AI requires vast resources, particularly water for cooling data centers. According to the World Economic Forum, the standard 1 megawatt (MW) data center can guzzle approximately 25.5 million liters of water per year; this is comparable to the daily consumption of 300,000 residents in a medium-sized city in Vietnam. The energy implications of such resource consumption are stark. Diverting natural resources to cool AI’s growing infrastructure threatens to deplete local and regional water reserves. This strain on Vietnam’s environment is escalating in what the World Bank already views as one of the most at-risk countries for global climate change and rising coastal waters.
More importantly, the new law fails to offer any social protections for workers and communities who are displaced by AI technology. Across Asia, for example, workers in the gig economy have protested companies that control AI-generated algorithms, which have tightened delivery times while cutting wages. Vietnam has clearly missed an opportunity to take a more worker-friendly, human-centric approach to AI regulation. It is not alone in this; governments across the region have generally shirked any meaningful effort to provide a social safety net to support workers from a growing wave of AI systems and robotic automation.
These shortcomings collectively underscore how during periods of great transformation, various stakeholders, including countries, companies, and local communities, must cooperate to protect two essential commodities that are central to the global economy; namely, land and labor. Consequently, Vietnam’s AI law, and others like it that fail to address governance gaps involving key commodities and regulatory coordination, will undermine AI’s overall effectiveness, exacerbating economic dislocation and social displacement that could potentially unleash regional instability and uncertainty for many years to come.
