articles.title: Pakistan, China Sign $850 Million Deals to Boost Pharmaceutical Cooperation
articles.full_text:
The costs of Pakistan’s dependence on imports for medicines and vaccines are huge. Chinese investment could end this reliance.
Health workers vaccinate a 2-year-old child during a polio vaccination campaign in January 2015 in a rural area of Tehsil Fateh Jang, Punjab in Pakistan.
Last week, Pakistan and Chinese companies signed agreements worth $850 million at the Pakistan-China Pharmaceutical and Healthcare B2B Investment Conference in Islamabad.
Held on July 17 and 18, the event focused on vaccine production, active pharmaceutical ingredients (API), medical devices, clinical trials, and related pharmaceutical subsectors. It brought together 146 Chinese companies with around 220 delegates and more than 200 Pakistani firms, marking one of the largest China-Pakistan business engagements in the pharmaceutical, healthcare, and biotechnology sectors.
Federal Health Minister Mustafa Kamal announced on July 18 that 16 contracts and 80 memoranda of understanding had been finalized during the event. He termed the development a key economic milestone for cooperation between China and Pakistan in the pharmaceutical sector. The deals signed and the scope of the expected cooperation mark a clear shift toward industrial collaboration between the two countries, beyond the limited trade exchanges of earlier years.
Notably, Pakistan’s dependence on imported vaccines and pharmaceutical inputs remains critical. For instance, the country administers 13 vaccines under its national immunization program, and all these vaccines are imported. Moreover, while Pakistan manufactures about 85 percent of its finished medicines locally, it imports around 95 percent of the API required to produce them. The country’s dependency also extends to imports for essential vaccines and specialized medicines. This essentially means that Pakistan’s healthcare system is vulnerable to global shipping delays, currency shifts, cuts in foreign aid, and changes in donors’ priorities.
For its 240 million people, the consequences of vaccine import dependency are huge.
For instance, vaccine-preventable diseases, such as measles, diphtheria, polio, and rabies continue to affect people, especially children. At times, shortages and delayed shipments force health authorities to ration doses or postpone campaigns. In other cases, thousands of children die every year in Pakistan simply due to non-vaccination because their parents do not pay any heed to the importance of immunization. In this context, a lack of awareness and persistent vaccine shortages highlight a long-standing challenge within Pakistan’s pharmaceutical sector.
The government, it seems, is now pursuing broader pharmaceutical reforms with Chinese support to open an industry that has remained underdeveloped for a long time.
For the first time, Pakistan has approved a National Local Vaccine Production Policy. Arguably, the policy has set the framework for domestic vaccine manufacturing with assistance from Chinese companies. The policy seeks to build local production capacity, strengthen health security, and cut dependence on imported medicines and vaccines.
In this regard, the Chinese investment and technology transfer that is envisaged under the recent agreements could reshape the pharma sector. This is the first time that such substantial investment pledges and private-sector collaboration are happening with full support from the governments of both countries.
Pakistan is facing recurrent vaccine shortages and systemic challenges that severely undermine its immunization efforts. The economic costs of importing medicines intensify these challenges. Pakistan’s medicine and vaccine import costs run into hundreds of millions of dollars each year. It is estimated that the annual bill for imported vaccines could reach $1.2 billion by 2030. The planned local production could help Pakistan reduce imports and save foreign exchange.
Moreover, agreements have been reached with Chinese companies to produce raw materials domestically, which would further lower medicine prices and benefit the Pakistani public.
No other country apart from China has shown this level of interest in Pakistan’s pharmaceutical sector. Agreements signed at the conference include two in API manufacturing, eight in vaccine production, two in clinical trials, two in generic formulation injectables, and eight in medical devices. This could dramatically change Pakistan’s healthcare sector if implemented fully.
The deals struck recently pave the way for local production and knowledge transfer in the coming years.
As part of the agreements, Chinese firms are set to establish plants in Pakistan through joint ventures, co-produce raw materials, and build new industrial capacity that will also create jobs locally. Many of these units are expected to be built in special economic zones that are being developed under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, where targeted policy incentives are expected to accelerate industrial growth.
That said, Chinese private investors might still face regulatory and other obstacles in research and development. The Pakistani government must provide a competitive and transparent environment that is free from political instability and regulatory confusion if the partnership is to deliver results. An opportunity like this may not come again and should be taken seriously by the federal government.

articles.title: Kashagan Environmental Fine Enforced in Kazakhstan
articles.full_text:
An asset freeze could be the first step of an acrimonious fight with the foreign oil majors developing one of the country’s largest oil fields.
Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Justice imposed a freeze on property and transport assets owned by the North Caspian Operating Company (NCOC), which is developing one of the country’s largest oil fields, over failure to pay a massive environmental fine.
The decision followed a back-and-forth between the government and NCOC, a collection of international oil companies drilling for oil at Kashagan, an offshore field in the Caspian Sea.
The July 21 decision was disclosed only three days later, and it remains unclear exactly what kind of property or transport assets were affected.
Also on July 21, according to Reuters sources, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Justice told NCOC’s managing director Giancarlo Ruiu that he would be held responsible for “administrative and criminal liability for non-compliance.”
In 2023, a local court imposed a 2.3 trillion tenge ($4.9 billion) fine for improper sulfur storage on the consortium.
The fine, alongside a dispute over a number of provisions in the contract between the government and NCOC, became a bone of contention within much larger arbitration proceedings. 
Kazakhstan’s government claims that the conditions of the Kashagan contract are unfair and is now asking for a recalculation of the costs and a higher share of the profits. The claim, according to sources familiar with the arbitration proceedings, is worth around $165 billion.
On July 20, Kazakhstan’s Kazmunaigas, which owns 16.88 percent of NCOC, offered to pay its part of the environmental fine, insiders told Bloomberg.
The international partners in the consortium, meanwhile, refused. Shell, Eni, TotalEnergies, and ExxonMobil each hold a 16.81 percent stake, while China’s CNPC (8.33 percent) and Japan’s Inpex (7.65 percent) own the rest.
Given the complex and lengthy legal dispute, a UNCITRAL tribunal rejected Kazakhstan’s request to lift restraining measures on the enforcement of the environmental fine, which are in place as long as the arbitration between the parties remains pending.
Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Justice replied that the United Nations tribunal cannot limit its sovereign rights to enforce the fine.
“An interim order in a commercial arbitration proceeding under UNCITRAL rules does not have automatic effect in Kazakhstan and does not limit the state’s exercise of its sovereign powers to protect the environment and public interests,” an official note said.
Under Kazakhstan’s new Constitution, hastily approved via referendum on March 15 and in force since July 1, domestic laws have precedence over international obligations.
The foreign companies, meanwhile, said that they “consider the sulfur fine to be without any basis and are contesting it by all available means.”
In 2022, Kazakhstan levied a fine alleging that NCOC had breached its sulfur storage permits. Sulfur is a toxic byproduct of oil extraction and can be used as a component for fertilizers. NCOC sells most of its sulfur to Chinese importers, but a temporary ban on exports led to excessive amounts being stored in addition to the existing stockpile in the summer of 2022.
In the past, environmental fines have been used by the government of Kazakhstan to push for better conditions or a revision of existing agreements. Analysts argued that these fines are, in fact, political tools. 
In 2011, Kazakhstan’s government threatened an environmental fine against Karachaganak, a major gas and condensate field. The consortium sold off a 10 percent stake to Kazmunaigas and the fine disappeared. Seven years later, the foreign consortium operating Karachaganak agreed to pay Kazakhstan a $1.1 billion compensation to end all existing disputes. And yet, in January 2026, the government once again knocked at Karachaganak’s door and asked for an additional $4 billion.
The Kashagan deal was struck in 1997 and further amended in 2008. The contract, much like the one signed for Karachaganak, is a so-called production sharing agreement (PSA), which legal experts deem favorable toward private investors. 
According to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists, Kazakhstan’s 2023 arbitral claim stated that NCOC “currently receives 98 percent of all post-Priority Payment revenue from oil production”
Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev repeatedly urged the government to renegotiate better terms for the PSA and joint venture contracts that concern the largest oil fields. 
According to analysts, there are ongoing talks of contract overhauls for the three largest oil fields, including Tengiz and Karachaganak. Together, these fields produce the vast majority of Kazakhstan’s oil and represent major tax and hard currency contributors to the country’s budget.

articles.title: Why Australia Struggles to Foster Asia Experts
articles.full_text:
A new government report looks at Australia’s “Asia capability” and finds the country wanting.
Earlier this month, the Australian government published an inquiry into the development of the country’s Asia capability titled “Security and Prosperity in Asia: Building Asia Capability in Australia through the Education System and Beyond.” The capability this inquiry sought to evaluate includes the teaching and learning of Asian languages and cultures, alongside how best to facilitate the public’s broader regional engagement. 
The report argued that Australia’s prosperity, diplomacy, and strategic independence increasingly depend on Australians developing stronger knowledge of the Asian region; yet the institutions responsible for building this capability are weakening. Without a public who have a good ability to understand and engage effectively with Asia, there is a diminished capacity for Australia to advance itself and secure its future. 
The report distinguished between general Asia literacy for the broader population and the deeper specialist expertise required for diplomats, researchers, business leaders, defense officials, and policymakers. Yet the former feeds into the latter. Without a high baseline of knowledge within the general public, it is more difficult for the country to produce the critical mass of experts required to do the specialist roles. Schools should provide all students with a strong general knowledge of the region, and then universities can hone this into producing highly skilled experts with advanced knowledge. 
The report highlighted that this pipeline is exhibiting serious problems. It presented evidence that fewer Australians are studying Asian languages than in previous decades, particularly in languages deemed to be the priority for the Australian government – Indonesian, Japanese, and Mandarin. These have fallen sharply in secondary schools, and declined dramatically at universities. 
The study of Indonesian was singled out as facing a crisis. Indonesia is Australia’s largest near neighbor, so strategically it should be considered a vital subject. Yet the report described study of the Indonesian language as approaching “functional extinction” within the education systems of some states. 
This decline risks having a compounding effect. With fewer students studying Asian languages at school, universities will reduce or close language programs due to low demand. This then diminishes the number of future teachers, academics, and researchers required to sustain the system. The report warned that Australia risks losing the institutional capacity to build the Asia expertise it requires. 
There are some structural hurdles that Australia faces. The first is that responsibility of building Asia capabilities is fragmented across schools, universities, state governments, federal departments, and businesses. Because no single institution oversees the system as a whole, there is little coordination between school language programs, university pathways, workforce needs, and national strategic priorities. 
Despite the report being chaired by a government MP, former Assistant Minister for Foreign Affairs Tim Watts, the report highlighted the absence of national leadership from the federal government. 
The other structural hurdles are cultural, and this has two components. First, there is a deep complacency within the Australian psyche that restricts the country from investing in key capacities. It has long been identified that Australia has prospered from luck rather than effort, and this has bred an ingrained lethargic culture that prevents the country from engaging in foresight and preparedness. 
The second cultural problem is one of suspicion toward the region. While Australia has become a highly multicultural society and this has created strong diaspora links within Asia, there remains a cohort of people in the country who do not see the merit in developing greater cultural knowledge of the region and often see this as a threat. The current rise of the One Nation party especially can be viewed as a revolt against the country’s geography. 
Yet the thing about geography is that it cannot be changed. Mature countries understand their geographic positions and seek to take advantage of them. Australia’s run of extraordinary luck hasn’t ended, as the world’s economic center of gravity has shifted to the Indo-Pacific. That provides the country with a wealth of opportunities should it develop the skills to harness them. 
The report argued that advances in AI or translation technology are no solution, that instead these are lazy ways to address the capability deficit. These digital tools are unable to replace deeper cultural understanding, contextual knowledge, and the human relationships necessary for diplomacy, economic opportunity, and broader regional engagement. 
For once, Australians may be required to do some actual work. The report offered 34 recommendations that can create a path forward for Australia to enhance its Asia capabilities. These fall short of making priority languages compulsory school subjects, but they do present a blueprint for improvements. Yet these recommendations may still be futile if Australia cannot confront its own cultural resistance and lack of political will.

articles.title: Asia’s Overlooked Maritime Flashpoints
articles.full_text:
Besides the South China Sea, there are various waterways under contention, from open ocean to marshlands and rivers.
Sir Creek and the India-Pakistan coastal borderlands.
You’ve probably heard of the South China Sea disputes – a major flashpoint involving China, the Philippines, Vietnam, and others. But the South China Sea isn’t the only maritime dispute in Asia. 
Today, we’re going to talk about four often-overlooked maritime flashpoints in South and Southeast Asia – and how they’re reshaping the geopolitical landscape today. 
In East Asia, various states are mostly fighting over who owns particular rocks in order to claim control of the surrounding ocean. Things are different in South and Southeast Asia. Besides the South China Sea, there are various waterways under contention, from open ocean to marshlands and rivers. Even settled maritime borders are becoming problems thanks to changing political circumstances on the water and on land.
But which of these maritime flashpoints are most likely to lead to an actual conflict? Let’s dive in.

articles.title: Thailand Says Goodbye to the ‘Land Bridge’ — For Now
articles.full_text:
A government feasibility study found what many already expected: that the project’s financial returns did not justify the massive capital outlay.
In late April, Sebastian Strangio and I penned separate articles for The Diplomat highlighting how Thailand’s ambition to build a “land bridge” across its upper southern provinces as an alternative trade route to the Strait of Malacca – via two deep-sea ports linked by a dual-track railway and a six-lane motorway – was increasingly framed by Thai leaders as an imperative amid deepening geopolitical volatility. What we said lost relevance quickly, with the shelving of the one-trillion-baht megaproject coming to light on July 24.
The announcement was made verbally by Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas, citing unfavorable findings in a government feasibility study. Just as too many skeptics have loudly reasoned, the projected financial return does not look promising. The operational requirement to repeatedly load and unload goods is too much of a hassle and may end up taking more time than shipping through the supposedly longer Malacca route.
Another guaranteed problem is environmental damage. Constructing a 90-kilometer transport corridor entails seaward land reclamation of roughly 13,000 rai in two ecologically rich provinces: 7,000 rai in Ranong on the Andaman Coast and 6,000 rai in Chumphon facing the Gulf of Thailand. This far exceeds 5,257 rai (2,411 during Phase 1 and 2 construction, and 2,846 as part of the unfinished Phase 3 expansion) of sea area reclaimed for Laem Chabang Port, Thailand’s main international deep-sea terminal in the Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC).
In place of the land bridge, a downsized infrastructure upgrade will be directed to the area most in need, namely Ranong. The existing Ranong Port will be modernized, and it will have a direct rail connection to the national train network already running through Chumphon.
Advancing Ranong as Thailand’s logistics gateway to the Indian Ocean makes structural sense. First, Ranong has both strong coastal and inland connectivity, with the nearest distance to the capital Bangkok of any Andaman province, not to mention the close proximity to Myanmar. Second, Ranong is the sole Andaman province to have its port managed by the Port Authority of Thailand, the administrator of key state-owned commercial ports, including Laem Chabang. Phuket, despite being the poster child of the Andaman region and having its own deep-sea port near the Royal Thai Navy’s Third Naval Area Command, is too tourism-oriented and has limited capacity for expansion, in a literal physical sense.
As Ekniti stressed, stopping the land bridge project comes with no monetary loss since neither land acquisition nor actual construction has begun. The effect has purely been reputational for the Thai government, both good and bad.
The Thai public has opposed the land bridge, fiercely so over the past few months. Beyond environmental concerns discussed earlier, fear of excessive foreign capital flooding in is a crucial factor. Many have probably harbored an expectation that the government of Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul would be stubborn, considering its action-oriented image and the high-profile promotion of the land bridge by successive Thai administrations since 2023. The Anutin government’s ultimate decision to scrap the project, then, could be viewed positively as a responsive move. Some netizens, such as those commenting on the Facebook page of a popular economic blog Longtunman, apparently think along this line.
At the same time, heavily promoting the land bridge to international investors when its viability has always been questionable reflects poorly on Thailand’s credibility. It does not help that other major infrastructure promises have stalled. The high-speed rail linking three airports (U-Tapao, Suvarnabhumi, and Don Mueang), a critical component of the EEC, has not taken shape since the contract was signed in 2019. The long-floated plan to build the Andaman airport in Phang Nga province to relieve congestion in neighboring Phuket remains stuck on paper. An even older proposal suffering the same fate is the one for Phuket’s light rail transit system.
To be fair, these projects are prone to unforeseen circumstances like the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as structural complexities. In the case of Phuket, for instance, even a minor transport infrastructure upgrade could paralyze part of the island, given there is only one main highway. Yet there is a natural tendency to pay selective attention, and execution seems to be all that matters in rating how credible a government is.
With the centuries-old idea of digging a canal across the Kra Isthmus resurfacing time and again, the land bridge, as a strategically safer proposal rooted in the same concept, could very well make a return. A successful modernization of Ranong Port will be the vital first step.

articles.title: Vietnam Planning Social Media Restrictions for Children Under 16
articles.full_text:
The proposed rules would would bar minors from posting, sharing, or commenting on social media platforms.
Vietnam is set to order social media platforms to limit the access of children under 16 to social media, becoming the latest nation and the third in Southeast Asia to tighten online safety provisions for minors.
According to a draft amendment to a decree on internet management, the new rules would bar children under the age of 16 from posting, commenting, sharing, or reacting on social media, leaving them able only to view content, Vietnamese state media reported on Friday.
At a meeting to discuss the new rules the day prior, Nguyen Thi Thanh Huyen, deputy director of the Authority of Broadcasting and Electronic Information, said that accounts belonging to under-16s would have to be registered using a parent’s or guardian’s information. That adult “would then be responsible for supervising the content the child sees and the time they spend on the platform,” the report stated.
“A child’s account, under the supervision of parents or guardians, can only view content. It cannot post, interact, comment, or share,” Huyen said.
At the same time, social media companies will also be tasked with identifying child users and ensure that they are exposed only to age-appropriate content, Reuters reported, citing copy of the draft amendment.
Unlike in Australia, which introduced the world’s first social media ban for under 16s last year, the measures will stop short of a full prohibition.
“The primary objective is not to ban or excessively restrict children’s access ​to social media, but rather to ensure that when children use social media services, they are placed in an age-appropriate environment and protected from inappropriate risks,” Deputy Culture Minister Phan Tam said ​at Thursday’s meeting.
The measures align Vietnam with a growing effort to restrict minors’ access to social media platforms, in the interests of protecting them from cyberbullying, online fraud, and exposure to pornography, among other perceived threats. The draft decree also proposes new ​restrictions on ⁠online gaming, according to Reuters. These would require game operators to verify users’ ages, register under-16 accounts through a parent or guardian, and limit children ⁠to no more than 60 minutes of play ​per day.
Vietnam has the seventh-largest pool of Facebook users in the world, with some 89 million accounts registered as of last month. It also has an estimated TikTok audience of approximately 80 million.
These moves follow Australia’s introduction of the world’s first social media ban for under 16s. The policy, which took effect in December, forces social media firms to block users under 16 from having accounts on their platforms, rather than penalizing young people or their parents.
A long list of countries, including India, China, Türkiye, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and several European nations (most recently France), have since announced the introduction of curbs of some kind.
Within Southeast Asia, Indonesia on March 28 became the first nation to ban under 16s from having accounts on what it termed “high-risk” digital platforms, which include YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, Threads, X, Bigo Live, and Roblox. Malaysia started enforcing a similar ban on June 1.
In all of these cases, the efficacy of such restrictions remains to be seen. Recent evidence from Australia suggests that the social media ban has been undermined by “limited implementation, incomplete compliance, and substantial circumvention of social media restrictions.” Last month, the Australian government announced that it would double the penalty for breaches of the ban to A$99 million, after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that “there are still too many children on social media.”
While Vietnam’s proposed approach seems to strike a sensible balance between a full ban and a total lack of regulation, Facebook’s parent company Meta suggested that the technical challenges of enforcing this might be considerable.
Nguyen Thu Thao, Meta’s public policy director for Vietnam, told VnExpress that platforms identify likely child accounts by identifying behavioral patterns in how they interact with the platform.
“If children use social media only passively, platforms will no longer have the behavioral signals they need to identify a user as a child,” Thao said. This would then weaken Facebook’s ability to detect and protect children online.

articles.title: Philippines Holds Joint Exercises With US, Japan in South China Sea Amid Tensions With China
articles.full_text:
Manila and Beijing continue to trade accusations about a series of clashes at two disputed features in the South China Sea last week.
In this photo released by the Philippine military, Filipino sailors take part in the 17th Multilateral Maritime Cooperative Activity, a joint exercise with the United States and Japan, which took place in the South China Sea on July 21-25, 2026.
The Philippines on Saturday wound up a series of joint maritime exercises with the United States and Japan in the South China Sea, against a backdrop of tension between Philippine and Chinese vessels at two disputed features.
The 17th Multilateral Maritime Cooperative Activity, which began on July 21, brought together warships, coast guard vessels, and surveillance and fighter aircraft, the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) said in a statement yesterday.
“Throughout the five-day activity, participating forces carried out a series of advanced maritime interoperability exercises,” the AFP said. These included communication exercises, replenishment at sea operations, and division tactics.
The exercises underscored “the enduring partnership among the partner nations in promoting peace, stability, and security in the Indo-Pacific region,” it stated. They also reflected the AFP’s “continuing commitment in ensuring freedom of navigation and overflight while deterring illegal, coercive, aggressive, and deceptive activities” in the South China Sea. The Philippine military did not disclose the exact location of the exercises.
The drills took place at a time of resurgent tensions in the contested seaway, which have coincided with the 10th anniversary of the South China Sea arbitral ruling, handed down by a special tribunal in The Hague, that found China’s expansive “nine-dash line” claim in the South China Sea had no basis under international law. China does not recognize the ruling, saying that it is “null and void.”
On Friday, the Philippine accused the China Coast Guard (CCG) of firing water cannon ‌at its vessels near Scarborough Shoal for the second day. The Philippine Coast Guard said that the incident took place while the PCG and Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources were delivering fuel and provisions to Filipino fishing boats, part of a national initiative “to ensure the safety and security of Filipino fisherfolk exercising their legitimate rights in their traditional fishing ground.”
The water cannons hit both PCG and BFAR vessels with the high-pressure water streams while a separate CCG vessel came within about 7 meters of ​a BFAR boat, creating “a serious risk of collision.” The PCG also released several videos that it claims showed the water cannon incidents.
“The PCG strongly condemns the dangerous and unprofessional actions of ​the China Coast Guard,” PCG spokesperson Jay Tarriela said in the statement. Scarborough Shoal, which lies within the Philippines’ 200-nautical-mile Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), was a traditional ⁠fishing ground of Filipinos, “whose rights cannot be lawfully impeded by any foreign power,” he said. The National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea described the actions as “unlawful and dangerous.”
The CCG in turn accused the Philippines of organizing several government and PCG vessels, along with a large number of fishing vessels, to “illegally gather” around the shoal, which China refers to as Huangyan Dao. It said that it had taken legal measures to warn, block, and deploy water cannon after the official vessels ​from the Philippines ignored those measures from the CCG and “insisted on intruding.”
A similar confrontation took place at Scarborough Shoal on Thursday, when the PCG accused its Chinese counterpart of undertaking “illegal, coercive, and aggressive actions,” including the use of water cannons, to disrupt a supply mission. The CCG countered by urging the Philippines to “immediately cease its infringing and provocative actions,” and reasserting China’s sovereignty over the disputed shoal.
Lying around 200 kilometers to the west of the Philippines’ Luzon island, and 874 kilometers from China’s Hainan Island, Scarborough Shoal has been a persistent flashpoint in the maritime disputes between the Philippines and China. The shoal has been under Chinese control since a stand-off between the two sides in 2012, and the CCG regularly stations vessels around the triangular atoll. In recent years, they have made repeated attempts to restrict Filipino fishermen from accessing the rich fishing grounds inside the atoll’s central lagoon.
The two incidents at Scarborough Shoal followed an incident on July 20 at Second Thomas Shoal in the Spratly Islands, some 650 kilometers away, in which Philippine and Chinese personnel exchanged direct physical blows. The Philippines said that one of its personnel sustained a head injury after being struck with a baton by CCG personnel who had deployed in a boat close to the BRP Sierra Madre, the grounded warship that serves as Manila’s outpost on the shoal.
As in the above cases, China accused the Philippines of transgressing into its waters, attempting to ram the Chinese patrol boat, and of spreading “false propaganda” about the incident. The incident came as ASEAN’s foreign ministers concluded a week of regional meetings in Manila, during which U.S. Secretary of ⁠State Marco Rubio described China’s actions in the South China Sea as “disturbing” and reaffirmed Washington’s support for its long-time security ally. Other Philippine partners expressed similar concerns about the incident.
The confrontation at Second Thomas Shoal also revived disagreements about a “provisional” understanding that Beijing and Manila reached after in June 2024, after a Filipino sailor lost a finger during a physical melee at the shoal. The agreement sought to reduce misunderstandings during missions intended to resupply the unit of marines stationed aboard the BRP Sierra Madre, and until this week, had largely succeeded in reducing tensions between the two sides.
Beijing accused Manila of transgressing the terms of the agreement, the terms of which were never published, during the July 20 incident. The Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs said on Thursday that the arrangement neither recognizes any foreign jurisdiction nor requires the Philippines to ask China for permission ​to carry out resupply ​missions. Nor does it concede the Philippines’ “sovereignty, sovereign rights, and jurisdiction,” a position that it said was “vindicated” by the 2016 arbitral ruling.
The Philippines on Saturday wound up a series of joint maritime exercises with the United States and Japan in the South China Sea, against a backdrop of tension between Philippine and Chinese vessels at two disputed features.
The 17th Multilateral Maritime Cooperative Activity, which began on July 21, brought together warships, coast guard vessels, and surveillance and fighter aircraft, the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) said in a statement yesterday.
“Throughout the five-day activity, participating forces carried out a series of advanced maritime interoperability exercises,” the AFP said. These included communication exercises, replenishment at sea operations, and division tactics.
The exercises underscored “the enduring partnership among the partner nations in promoting peace, stability, and security in the Indo-Pacific region,” it stated. They also reflected the AFP’s “continuing commitment in ensuring freedom of navigation and overflight while deterring illegal, coercive, aggressive, and deceptive activities” in the South China Sea. The Philippine military did not disclose the exact location of the exercises.
The drills took place at a time of resurgent tensions in the contested seaway, which have coincided with the 10th anniversary of the South China Sea arbitral ruling, handed down by a special tribunal in The Hague, that found China’s expansive “nine-dash line” claim in the South China Sea had no basis under international law. China does not recognize the ruling, saying that it is “null and void.”
On Friday, the Philippine accused the China Coast Guard (CCG) of firing water cannon ‌at its vessels near Scarborough Shoal for the second day. The Philippine Coast Guard said that the incident took place while the PCG and Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources were delivering fuel and provisions to Filipino fishing boats, part of a national initiative “to ensure the safety and security of Filipino fisherfolk exercising their legitimate rights in their traditional fishing ground.”
The water cannons hit both PCG and BFAR vessels with the high-pressure water streams while a separate CCG vessel came within about 7 meters of ​a BFAR boat, creating “a serious risk of collision.” The PCG also released several videos that it claims showed the water cannon incidents.
“The PCG strongly condemns the dangerous and unprofessional actions of ​the China Coast Guard,” PCG spokesperson Jay Tarriela said in the statement. Scarborough Shoal, which lies within the Philippines’ 200-nautical-mile Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), was a traditional ⁠fishing ground of Filipinos, “whose rights cannot be lawfully impeded by any foreign power,” he said. The National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea described the actions as “unlawful and dangerous.”
The CCG in turn accused the Philippines of organizing several government and PCG vessels, along with a large number of fishing vessels, to “illegally gather” around the shoal, which China refers to as Huangyan Dao. It said that it had taken legal measures to warn, block, and deploy water cannon after the official vessels ​from the Philippines ignored those measures from the CCG and “insisted on intruding.”
A similar confrontation took place at Scarborough Shoal on Thursday, when the PCG accused its Chinese counterpart of undertaking “illegal, coercive, and aggressive actions,” including the use of water cannons, to disrupt a supply mission. The CCG countered by urging the Philippines to “immediately cease its infringing and provocative actions,” and reasserting China’s sovereignty over the disputed shoal.
Lying around 200 kilometers to the west of the Philippines’ Luzon island, and 874 kilometers from China’s Hainan Island, Scarborough Shoal has been a persistent flashpoint in the maritime disputes between the Philippines and China. The shoal has been under Chinese control since a stand-off between the two sides in 2012, and the CCG regularly stations vessels around the triangular atoll. In recent years, they have made repeated attempts to restrict Filipino fishermen from accessing the rich fishing grounds inside the atoll’s central lagoon.
The two incidents at Scarborough Shoal followed an incident on July 20 at Second Thomas Shoal in the Spratly Islands, some 650 kilometers away, in which Philippine and Chinese personnel exchanged direct physical blows. The Philippines said that one of its personnel sustained a head injury after being struck with a baton by CCG personnel who had deployed in a boat close to the BRP Sierra Madre, the grounded warship that serves as Manila’s outpost on the shoal.
As in the above cases, China accused the Philippines of transgressing into its waters, attempting to ram the Chinese patrol boat, and of spreading “false propaganda” about the incident. The incident came as ASEAN’s foreign ministers concluded a week of regional meetings in Manila, during which U.S. Secretary of ⁠State Marco Rubio described China’s actions in the South China Sea as “disturbing” and reaffirmed Washington’s support for its long-time security ally. Other Philippine partners expressed similar concerns about the incident.
articles.summary: Manila and Beijing continue to trade accusations about a series of clashes at two disputed features in the South China Sea last week.
